module_title: Maintaining Your Solar Inverter and Battery System

lessons.title: Monthly Checkup: Cleaning Panels, Tightening Connections
lessons.body:
A monthly checkup keeps your solar system running at peak performance. Set aside one hour each month, preferably in the morning when the sun is not too hot. Start with the solar panels. Use a soft brush or cloth with plain water to remove dust, bird droppings, and leaves. Avoid soap or harsh chemicals; they can leave residue that reduces power. If panels are on a roof, be careful. Use a long-handled soft brush from the ground if possible. Check for shadows from new tree growth or buildings; trim branches if needed.

Next, inspect all wiring connections. Turn off the inverter and disconnect the battery bank before touching any wires. Use a screwdriver to gently tighten terminal screws on the charge controller, inverter, and battery. Loose connections cause resistance, heat, and power loss. Look for any burnt or discolored wires; replace them immediately. Check that cable insulation is not cracked or chewed by rodents. If you find damage, wrap with electrical tape as a temporary fix, but order a replacement.

Also check the mounting structure. Bolts can loosen from vibration or wind. Tighten any loose bolts on panel racks and the inverter bracket. Clean the inverter's air vents with a dry cloth or soft brush. Dust buildup can cause overheating. If your inverter has a cooling fan, listen for unusual noises. A squealing fan needs replacement soon.

Finally, test the system. Turn everything back on and check the inverter display for normal voltage and power output. Compare with last month's readings. If output has dropped by more than 10%, investigate further. Record all findings in your maintenance log. This monthly routine prevents small issues from becoming costly repairs.

lessons.title: Battery Watering and Terminal Cleaning for Flooded Batteries
lessons.body:
Flooded lead-acid batteries need regular watering to work properly. Check water levels every month, or every two weeks in hot, dry seasons. Use only distilled water, never tap water or rainwater. Tap water contains minerals that damage the battery plates. Remove the vent caps and look inside. The electrolyte level should cover the plates by about 1 cm (half an inch). If low, add distilled water until the level is just below the vent opening. Do not overfill; expansion can cause acid to spill.

Always wear safety glasses and rubber gloves. Battery acid is corrosive. If acid touches your skin, rinse with plenty of water and seek medical help. Work in a well-ventilated area; battery fumes are explosive. Never smoke or create sparks near batteries. Use a funnel to pour water to avoid spills. After watering, replace vent caps tightly.

Clean terminals every three months or when you see white or green powder (corrosion). Mix one tablespoon of baking soda in one cup of water. Dip a small brush in the solution and scrub the terminals and cable clamps. The mixture will fizz as it neutralizes acid. Wipe dry with a clean cloth. Then apply a thin layer of petroleum jelly or terminal protector spray to prevent future corrosion. Reconnect cables tightly; loose connections cause voltage drops and heat.

Check the battery case for cracks or leaks. If you find any, replace the battery. Test the specific gravity of each cell with a hydrometer. A fully charged cell reads about 1.265. If one cell reads much lower than others, that battery is failing. Record all readings in your log. Proper watering and cleaning can double battery life, saving you money.

lessons.title: Inverter Cooling and Dust Management in Dry Seasons
lessons.body:
Inverters generate heat during operation, especially when converting DC to AC. In hot, dusty African climates, cooling and dust control are critical. Most inverters have cooling fans and air vents. If dust blocks these, the inverter overheats, reduces power output, or shuts down. Clean the vents and fans every two weeks during dry seasons. Use a soft brush or vacuum with a brush attachment. Never use water or wet cloths inside the inverter; moisture causes short circuits.

Place the inverter in a shaded, well-ventilated area. Avoid direct sunlight; it can raise internal temperatures by 10â15Â°C. If the inverter is in a small room, install a vent or small exhaust fan. Ensure at least 30 cm (12 inches) of clearance around the unit for airflow. Do not stack items on top of the inverter. In dusty regions, consider building a simple enclosure with dust filters, but make sure it does not block airflow. Clean or replace filters monthly.

Listen for the cooling fan. If it runs constantly or makes grinding noises, it may be failing. A replacement fan is inexpensive and easy to install for a technician. You can also check the inverter's temperature reading on its display. If it regularly exceeds 60Â°C (140Â°F), improve ventilation immediately. Some inverters have a 'derating' feature that reduces power when hot; this is normal but reduces your backup time.

During the hottest months, you can help by running heavy loads (like irons or water pumps) in the early morning or evening when temperatures are lower. Keep the area around the inverter free of dust, cobwebs, and insects. A clean, cool inverter lasts longer and performs better. Add cooling checks to your monthly log.

lessons.title: Recognizing Warning Signs: Beeping, Overheating, Reduced Backup
lessons.body:
Your inverter and battery communicate problems through warning signs. Learn to recognize them early to avoid costly damage. Beeping is the most common alert. A continuous beep often means low battery voltage or overload. A short beep every few seconds may indicate a fault code. Check the inverter manual for specific beep patterns. If the inverter beeps during a power outage, it is warning that battery is low; reduce load immediately by turning off non-essential appliances.

Overheating is another critical sign. If the inverter feels too hot to touch, or if it shuts down automatically, it is overheating. Check for blocked vents, failed fans, or direct sunlight. Allow it to cool, then clean vents and improve ventilation. Never pour water on a hot inverter. Overheating shortens electronic component life. If overheating continues after cleaning, call a technician.

Reduced backup time is a gradual warning. If your battery used to run lights for 8 hours but now only lasts 3 hours, the battery is weakening. This can be due to age, sulfation, or undercharging. Check water levels (for flooded batteries) and charging settings. A battery that is 3â5 years old may need replacement. Also, check for loose connections or corroded terminals, which cause voltage drops. If one battery in a bank is weak, it drags down the whole bank. Test each battery individually with a multimeter.

Other signs include a burning smell, flickering lights, or error codes on the display. A burning smell means immediate shutdown and professional inspection. Flickering lights often indicate poor connections or an overloaded inverter. Write down any error codes and when they occur. This information helps a technician diagnose quickly. Never ignore warning signs; early action saves money and prevents fire hazards.

lessons.title: Keeping a Maintenance Log for Your Business
lessons.body:
A maintenance log is a simple notebook or spreadsheet where you record all checks, repairs, and observations. For a solar business, it is essential for tracking performance, planning replacements, and proving reliability to customers. Use a dedicated exercise book or a free app like Google Sheets. Create columns for date, task performed, readings (voltage, water levels, specific gravity), issues found, and actions taken. Keep the log near the inverter for easy access.

Every time you do a monthly checkup, write down the date and what you did. For example: '5 Jan 2025 â Cleaned panels, tightened battery terminals, water levels OK, inverter temp 45Â°C.' If you add water, note how much per cell. If you clean corrosion, note it. Record any unusual sounds, smells, or error codes. Also log the weather; dust and heat affect performance. After a power outage, note how long the battery lasted and what loads were running. This data helps you calculate actual backup time.

Over months, patterns emerge. You might see that battery water needs topping up more often in the dry season, or that inverter temperature rises when you run the welding machine. These insights let you adjust usage or schedule maintenance. The log also helps when you call a technician: you can show exactly what happened and when. For a business, the log is a record of asset care. If you sell your system, a well-kept log increases its value. It also helps with warranty claims; manufacturers often ask for maintenance records.

Make log-keeping a habit. At the end of each month, review the log and plan the next month's tasks. Train employees to fill it in. A simple log takes five minutes but can save thousands in repairs. It turns guesswork into informed decisions.

lessons.title: When to Call a Technician vs Fix It Yourself
lessons.body:
Knowing when to fix a problem yourself and when to call a technician saves time, money, and prevents danger. You can safely handle routine maintenance: cleaning panels, tightening connections, watering batteries, cleaning terminals, and checking log readings. These tasks require basic tools like a screwdriver, multimeter, hydrometer, and soft brush. Always turn off the system before working on wiring. If you are unsure, do not proceed.

Call a technician for any electrical work inside the inverter or charge controller. These devices store dangerous voltages even after shutdown. Opening the casing voids warranties and can cause electric shock. Also call a technician for battery bank rewiring, replacing faulty batteries, or installing new components. If you see sparks, smell burning, or hear loud buzzing, shut down the system and call a professional immediately. Do not attempt to repair a burnt circuit board or replace internal fuses unless you are trained.

Other signs you need a technician: persistent error codes that you cannot clear, inverter that repeatedly shuts down, or a battery that gets very hot during charging. If your system is under warranty, contact the installer first; DIY repairs may void it. For business owners, having a trusted technician on call is wise. Ask for recommendations from other solar users. A good technician will explain the problem and show you what they did. You can then handle similar issues in the future.

Finally, trust your instincts. If a task feels risky or you lack the right tools, call for help. The cost of a technician is far less than a fire or a ruined inverter. Keep emergency numbers posted near your system. Regular maintenance reduces the need for repairs, but when in doubt, professional help is the safest choice.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Maintaining Your Solar Inverter and Battery System

For any African small business running on solar â a maize mill, a cold room, a barbershop, a phone-charging kiosk, a poultry brooder â the inverter and battery bank are the engine of the enterprise. When they fail, income stops the same day. This practical reference gives you a repeatable maintenance routine you can run yourself, the warning signs that demand action, and a clear line between what you fix and what a technician must handle.

Two rules govern everything below. First, maintenance is cheaper than replacement: a flooded battery bank that lasts five years instead of two saves you the cost of an entire second bank. Second, most failures in African installations are preventable â dust, heat, loose terminals, and neglected water levels, not manufacturing defects.

Why a Maintenance Log Is a Business Tool, Not a Chore

Write down four things every month: date, action taken, battery voltage or state-of-charge reading, and any symptom you noticed. This single page of notes does three things for your business:

  • It predicts failure. If your log shows backup time dropping from 6 hours to 4 hours over three months, you know the battery is degrading before it dies on a busy Saturday.
  • It protects your warranty. Most inverter and battery warranties are void without proof of regular maintenance. A dated log is your evidence.
  • It saves technician fees. When you do call an expert, a clear log lets them diagnose in one visit instead of three.

Data Table 1: Monthly Maintenance Schedule and Time Budget

Task Frequency Time needed Who can do it
Clean PV panels (dust, droppings)Weekly in harmattan/dry season; monthly otherwise15â30 minOwner or staff
Inspect & tighten DC/AC connectionsMonthly20 minOwner (with insulated tools)
Check battery water level (flooded)Monthly20â40 minOwner or staff
Clean battery terminals, apply anti-corrosion greaseEvery 3 months30 minOwner
Clear inverter vents and fan areaMonthly (more often in dusty areas)10 minOwner or staff
Record voltage / state of charge in logMonthly (or weekly)5 minOwner
Full system inspection (torque, insulation, earthing)Annually2â3 hoursQualified technician

Frequency guidance compiled from manufacturer O&M manuals (Victron Energy, Schneider Electric, Luminous) and IRENA/SEforALL off-grid maintenance guidance for Sub-Saharan Africa.

Data Table 2: Warning Signs, Likely Cause, and Action

Symptom Likely cause Your action
Continuous beepingLow battery, overload, or fault codeReduce load, check battery voltage, read fault code in manual
Inverter hot to touch / fan running constantlyBlocked vents, high ambient heat, overloadClear vents, shade unit, reduce load; if it persists, call technician
Backup time reduced by >30%Battery ageing, sulphation, low waterCheck water, test each battery; plan replacement
White/green crust on terminalsCorrosion from acid vapourClean with baking soda solution, apply petroleum jelly
Battery plates exposed (flooded)Water not topped upTop up with distilled water only â never tap water
Burning smell or smokeLoose connection, short circuitSwitch off immediately, do not touch, call technician
Panels look dull/greyDust, soot, harmattan hazeWash early morning with soft brush and clean water

Symptomâcause mapping adapted from Victron Energy and Schneider Electric inverter/battery manuals, and from field guidance in the GOGLA off-grid solar quality assurance framework.

â  SAFETY WARNING â READ BEFORE YOU TOUCH ANYTHING

Battery banks store lethal energy even when the inverter is switched off. Never short a battery terminal with a tool, ring, or watch â a shorted 48 V, 200 Ah bank can melt metal and cause severe burns or an explosion. Always use insulated tools, remove jewellery, and wear eye protection and gloves when working near batteries. Flooded batteries release explosive hydrogen gas while charging â never smoke, weld, or create sparks nearby, and keep the battery room ventilated. Do not open the inverter casing; capacitors inside hold a dangerous charge long after disconnection. If you are unsure, stop and call a qualified technician.

When to Call a Technician vs Fix It Yourself

Fix it yourself: cleaning panels, topping up flooded cells with distilled water, brushing off dust, cleaning corroded terminals, tightening accessible terminal nuts to the manufacturer's torque, recording voltage readings, clearing ventilation.

Call a qualified technician: any burning smell, smoke, or sparking; repeated tripping or fault codes you cannot clear; opening the inverter casing; replacing batteries or reconfiguring the bank; earthing and surge-protection checks; inverter firmware or settings changes; anything involving mains AC wiring.

In most African markets, a good solar technician is reachable by phone. Build a relationship before you need one â ask for their number when you buy the system, and keep it in your maintenance log.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Panels cleaned with soft brush and clean water â early morning, never on hot glass.
  • â All accessible DC and AC terminals checked and tightened with insulated tools.
  • â Flooded battery cells topped up to the marked level with distilled water only.
  • â Battery terminals clean, dry, and lightly coated with petroleum jelly or terminal grease.
  • â Inverter vents and fan area free of dust; unit shaded and well ventilated.
  • â Battery voltage / state of charge recorded in the maintenance log.
  • â Any beeping, overheating, or reduced backup time noted and investigated.
  • â Technician contact number and warranty documents stored with the log.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • IRENA â Off-grid Renewable Energy publications and O&M guidance
  • GOGLA â Off-grid solar quality assurance and consumer protection resources
  • Victron Energy â Inverter, charger and battery manuals & downloads
  • SEforALL â Energy access and off-grid system resources
  • IEA â Africa Energy Outlook (context on reliability and access)

Prepared for Rise Africa Skills â course: Solar Inverters & Batteries, module: Maintaining Your Solar Inverter and Battery System. Always follow the specific manual for your inverter and battery make and model.
